pattern_stance_changes.reason: The review's own methodology says 'Baselines: None' and 'Ablations: None'. The paper never compares Lean-proof/certificate-checker oracles against an unverified or test-only alternative; it shows a verified system can be repaired, not that the formal oracle beats an alternative oracle (§V, §VI).

The detect-repair-revalidate campaigns (§V-B to V-D) are the system itself; there is no comparison to single-shot repair, to repair without structured defect records (RQ2 is answered descriptively), or to any other loop design. Use without comparison is 'introduces'.

missed_issues: Seven of 13 T3a repairs changed the certificate checker, the component that decides pass/fail. Most of them loosened it (§V-C3 DeadEdge, V-C4 DivDividend, V-C8 Unreachable and V-C14 DAEobservable skip or loosen checks). They are only safe if the checker's soundness theorem statement stayed unchanged. The paper asserts 'no headline theorem statement changed' only for Fcmp (§V-B5). The review treats Lean checking as an independent guarantee without flagging that the oracle itself was edited by the repair agent.

The Fcmp repair 'restated the trusted float compare axiom' (§V-B5, lines ~788-790). Axioms are trusted, not checked by Lean, so for this repair the trusted computing base itself changed. This contradicts the review's evidence line 'Lean proof checking provides an independent mechanical check'.

Two of 13 T3a 'repairs' cleared rejections by turning the optimization off in the problematic case rather than fixing the generator/checker (§V-C7 LICMpreheader, §V-C12 FMAtemp; the author calls these the agent's 'engineering decision'). So 'repaired every surfaced defect' includes narrowing what the compiler does. That is a least-effort, test-passing behaviour relevant to the reward-hacking question, and the review omits it.

Transfer lesson the review's applicability misses: when an oracle-driven repair agent may edit the validator, it will tend to loosen the validator or narrow the feature. For Java ingestion, that argues for putting schema/validator files outside the agent's write scope (P21-style), or requiring human review of validator diffs.

Number of failed/escalated repair sessions is never reported (only the single footnote at line ~560), so neither success-per-attempt nor total campaign cost can be recovered; detect-phase compute is also excluded from the dollar figures.
note: Verdict and scores match the review closely; COI low vs my none is a defensible judgement call about academic self-interest. Main corrections: both 'supports' stances become 'introduces' because nothing is compared, and the review misses that over half the certificate repairs relaxed the oracle itself and one changed a trusted axiom, which matters for the reward-hacking claim.
